subject: Underlying values of Y* for every respondent

messages.author: 0d5c994b344af3a8
messages.subject: Underlying values of Y* for every respondent
parts:
Hello All

I have a  path model with categorical (ordinal) endogenous variables.  
M <- as.ordered(M)   ! M is actually dichotomous
Y <- as.ordered(Y)
Model '
M ~ X1 
Y ~ M+X2 
'

(1) I want the values of underlying latent variables M* and Y* for each and every response. How do I get those?

(2) My project objective is to calculate the effect of M on Y. I want to calculate the probabilities of falling in a particular category of Y when M=1 and when M=0. However, the coefficient of M in the second equation is actually the coefficient of M* which is a continuous variable and no longer a 0/1 dichotomous. How do I calculate the effect in such a scenario?

Thanks a lot for your time

Gouri

> when M=1 and when M=0. However,
> the coefficient of M in the second equation is actually the coefficient of M* which is acontinuous variable and no longer a 0/1 dichotomous.

Exactly the same as in probit regression. See any textbook on
categorical data-analysis.

Yves.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Underlying values of Y* for every respondent
parts: Can you elaborate why one cannot estimate the individual values of M* and Y*? How is the mean and SD of M* otherwise estimated?

They aren't.  The mean/SD of the underlying distribution are assumed fixed by necessity, usually to be standard normal (mu = 0, sigma = 1; this is the "delta" parameterization), but instead of assuming the total variance of M* is 1, you could assume the residual variance of M* is 1 (this is called the "theta" parameterization).  Using one of those assumptions, the thresholds are estimated as the z-scores corresponding the the cumulative probabilities implied by the observed sample proportions in each category.  You see values for the (residual) variances and (total) scales of y* (i.e., the SD of M* and Y*) in the lavaan summary output, but no standard errors because they are fixed rather than estimated.  

You can estimate the M and SD of the latent responses in situations such as multigroup or longitudinal models, where you constrain thresholds to be equal over time or across groups (to test strong measurement invariance), and any difference in the observed sample proportions in each category is assumed to be due to differences/changes in the M/SD of the latent response(s).  Here are a couple of places you can start reading:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

http://ibg.colorado.edu/cdrom2012/boomsma/FactorAnalysis/PracticalMeasurementInvarianceOrdinal/Literature/Millsap2004.pdf

Terry

On 12/03/2015 03:51 AM, Gouri Shankar Mishra wrote:
> Thanks Yves for your response. Can you elaborate why one cannot estimate
> the individual values of M* and Y*?

We do not need to estimate the individual Y* values in order to estimate
its mean and variance.

But there is a way, if you really want to 'see' them. Or at least a
rough approximation of them. You can use the lavPredict() function with
the option type="yhat". This will first compute the latent variable
scores, and then, we can compute the (model-predicted) continuous values
for the observed indicators. These are similar (more or less) to the
(virtual) Y* values.

library(lavaan)
HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5",
"x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )
head( lavPredict(fit, type="yhat") )

Yves.

On Fri, Dec 18, 2015 at 4:58 AM, Gouri Shankar Mishra <...> wrote:
Terrence

Would you have any thoughts on my second question - restated here

M = f(X1)
Y2 = g(X1, M)  

M is a binary 0/1 variable which may be considered the treatment indicator. Y2 is an ordered categorical observed variables. X is exogenous. If I try to identify the above model, then MPLUS (or any other software would assume the underlying latent continuous variable variable). In theta parameterization, the error terms in both the above equations will be standardized to 1. MPLUS will estimate two ordered probit regressions with WLSMV estimator.  

 In my model, M is not an exogenous variable but has been "endogenized". As a result, in  equation 2, the underlying latent continuous variable of M is used as an explanatory variable. This implies that I cannot calculate the marginal probabilities of Y2 using 0/1 values of M and average values of X (as one would in single equation ordered probit model). Is that correct?

If yes, what are my options?

This is not an area I have much experience with, but Yves included some discussion of categorical endogenous variables in a mediation presentation, available here:

http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf


The example starting on slide 22 has a binary outcome and ordinal mediator, whereas yours is the reverse situation, but you might be able to generalize from there.  If not, he provides references for further reading. 

This is a general SEM question, so if you have any follow-up questions that aren't specifically about lavaan, SEMNET is the perfect place to post such a question (instead of sending an email to my personal account):

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html


Terrence
